name: Fast C++ CSV Parser
workload: Reading a generated 8-column CSV (id,city,state,category,amount,quantity,flag,note) of 500K or 5M rows with clean and quoted-field profiles, in a count-rows loop and a full read loop into std::string cells, warm cache, single parser worker, Google Benchmark median real time.
claimed_speedup: 500K clean: count rows 81.8 ms vs 146.5 ms (~1.8x, derived from page data), read 82.8 ms vs 164.9 ms (~2.0x, derived from page data); 500K quoted: count 118.8 ms vs 197.2 ms, read 136.2 ms vs 223.5 ms (~1.6x, derived from page data); 5M clean read 944.2 ms vs 1,087 ms (~1.15x, derived from page data). Reversed on 5M count (881.5 ms vs 547.6 ms for csv-parser), in materialization tables, and against csv-parser positional reads with 4+ parser workers.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.50 (Visual Studio 2026), C++20, CMake Release configuration (optimization flags implied by the Release config, not spelled out), AVX2 enabled, CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, Google Benchmark 1.8.5
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12400 (12 logical CPUs, ~2.5 GHz), Windows 11 Home 25H2, Samsung 990 EVO SSD
tradeoffs: Single header csv.h. Column count and types are fixed at compile time (read_header plus read_row with typed arguments), so there is no dynamic row model. Does not parse quoted fields with embedded line breaks (the comparison marks the multiline profile unsupported). Optional background I/O thread (needs pthread with GCC, or CSV_IO_NO_THREAD). The caller owns row materialization and any parallelism.
caveats: The benchmark is in the competitor's repo (csv-parser author), not the project's own, and it was written to show where csv-parser wins: fast-cpp-csv-parser loses the 5M-row count benchmark, both materialization tables and the 4+ worker positional-read comparison. Windows/MSVC only, one machine, Google Benchmark overhead included. The fast-cpp-csv-parser source is fetched from master at build time, so no commit is pinned. Optimization flags are implied by CMake Release rather than listed, so tier A is borderline. The README of fast-cpp-csv-parser itself has no numbers, and no measurement against the guessed std::getline baseline was found (dfglib's csvPerformanceRuns.md only compares it with dfglib's own readers).

name: PicoHTTPParser
workload: Parse one HTTP/1.1 GET request (9 headers including a Cookie, 430 bytes) 100000 times in a loop, headers not inspected, single thread, timing with clock().
claimed_speedup: 100000 request parses: picohttpparser 0.036571 s vs http-parser 0.289766 s, about 7.9x (derived from page data); the same page puts fast-http (Common Lisp) at 0.138 s and says picohttpparser is '3.7 times faster' than fast-http.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O3 for both bench.c programs; environment listed as 'GCC version 6.0 (clang-600.0.51)' (Apple clang on OS X). http_parser.o is produced by 'make' in the http-parser repo, whose current Makefile builds http_parser.o with -O3 (the 2014 Makefile was not checked).
hardware: MacBook Pro, OS X Mavericks, 3GHz Intel Core i7, 8GB RAM (exact CPU model not given)
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; HTTP/1 parser of H2O; used by Perl modules Plack, Starman, Starlet and Furl
tradeoffs: Stateless one-shot parser over a complete buffer: it allocates nothing and returns pointers into the caller's buffer, so the caller re-calls with the whole buffer after partial reads (prevbuflen hint) and no callbacks are offered. Also provides phr_parse_response, phr_parse_headers and phr_decode_chunked. http-parser is a streaming callback-driven state machine, so the two do not do identical work.
caveats: Independent measurement taken by the author of the fast-http Common Lisp parser (the page is a copy of the fukamachi/fast-http README at an older commit, and its note says an earlier chart was deleted 'because the benchmark was wrong'; the current upstream README no longer carries the picohttpparser rows). A microbenchmark of one request repeated 100000 times (about 37 ms for picohttpparser), clock() with float timestamps, 2014 hardware and compilers, single run. The http-parser run used null callbacks. The README command line for the picohttpparser run shows 'gcc ... http_parser.c bench.c', which looks like a copy-paste slip. The picohttpparser README's own benchmark is a PNG chart hosted on gyazo that could not be read here; the repo's bench.c times picohttpparser alone (10 million parses) with no competitor. CPU model is generic ('3GHz Intel Core i7'), which keeps this at B rather than A.

name: StreamTok (Static Analysis for Efficient Streaming Tokenization)
workload: Streaming tokenization of JSON, CSV, TSV, XML, YAML, FASTA, DNS-zone, and log-file grammars, plus a worst-case synthetic grammar family (a{0,k}b)|a on a 10MB input, comparing StreamTok against flex-generated C lexers (and also nom/plex/regex in Rust, Reps' algorithm, and ExtOracle)
claimed_speedup: "a 2x to 3x speedup over existing tokenization tools such as flex"; on the worst-case synthetic grammar family, StreamTok has O(1) time-per-symbol vs flex's O(k) backtracking, so the gap grows unboundedly with grammar parameter k
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2640 v4 @ 2.40GHz / 128GB RAM (RQ1-RQ2 experiments); AMD EPYC 7252 8-core @ 3.10GHz / 256GB RAM (RQ3-RQ6, including the flex throughput comparison)
tradeoffs: StreamTok's O(1)-per-symbol streaming algorithm only applies to tokenization grammars with bounded 'maximum token neighbor distance' (max-TND); grammars with unbounded max-TND (the paper found this true for ~32% of a 2669-grammar GitHub-sourced sample, including grammars for C, R, and SQL) fall back to non-constant behavior. Requires a static pre-analysis pass and building a tokenization-extension DFA via powerset construction, plus a bounded lookahead buffer.
caveats: Peer-reviewed ASPLOS '26 paper (Li, Yang, Mamouras, Rice University) with a detailed reproducible-looking experimental section (hardware stated, multiple RQs, figures with real numbers), but I could not locate a public StreamTok source/artifact repository on GitHub, and the paper does not state Rust compiler version or build flags, so it is capped at Tier B rather than A. All numbers are read directly from the paper text/figures for RQ3 (Figs. 8-10); I did not independently recompute any ratios.

name: flex
workload: Running generated C-language tokenizers (recognizing keywords) over a 28,088-line, 685K-character C input; run time of the scanner (snippet only).
claimed_speedup: AT&T lex 29.8 s vs flex 19.3 s with default full table compression (~1.5x, derived), 9.0 s with flex -cfe (~3.3x, derived), 7.8 s with flex -cf (~3.8x, derived); snippet also states a factor of about 3 over lex for a scanner of about the same size. Snippet only, see caveats.
compiler_and_flags: flex table options -cfe, -cf and default compression (1988 option syntax); AT&T lex; C compiler and flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; standard scanner generator shipped by Linux and BSD distributions
tradeoffs: Table-driven DFA scanners; the fastest modes (-Cf, -CF) trade large tables for speed. Matching NUL bytes is slow. Interactive scanners are slower. The -l lex-compatibility option is documented as a major performance loss. Lexer only, no Unicode-aware matching.
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: the lex vs flex timings were read from WebSearch result text attributed to a 1988 comp.compilers posting (compilers.iecc.com articles such as 88-04-001 or 90-11-063 appeared in the results); compilers.iecc.com is blocked by the egress proxy, so the page was never opened and the exact article could not be pinned, hence benchmark_url is null. Timings are from 1988 hardware and 1988 flex. The flex repository (README, NEWS, ONEWS, manual doc/flex.texi) contains no lex timings; its manual only says -f/-F is 'much faster (factor of 2-3)' than -C (flex against itself) and that -l compatibility costs performance. Search snippets also say re2c -b scanners are faster than flex -Cf ones. License text in COPYING is flex's own BSD-style wording (BSD-3-Clause-like, with a no-endorsement clause); the awesome-c list tags it BSD-2-Clause.

name: Gigatoken
workload: Encoding the openwebtext corpus (owt_train.txt, 11.9GB) with BPE tokenizers for ~23 model families (GPT-2, Llama 3/3.1/3.2/3.3/4, Qwen 2/2.5/3/3.5/3.6, DeepSeek V3/R1/V4, GLM 4/5, Phi-4, Gemma, Mistral, etc.); Gigatoken tokenizes the whole file unsplit while HF tokenizers gets the first 100MB and tiktoken the first 1GB, both pre-split on the document separator
claimed_speedup: GPT-2 on AMD EPYC 9565 dual-socket (144 cores): 24.53 GB/s vs HF tokenizers' 24.8 MB/s (989x) and tiktoken's 36.0 MB/s (681x); other tokenizer families range roughly 9x-1300x depending on model and CPU (Apple M4 Max and AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D tables also given); SentencePiece-based tokenizers (Gemma, Mistral, CodeLlama) show the smallest gains, ~7-22x

name: Pika Parser (reference implementation)
workload: (1) 2,500 random arithmetic expressions (integers, binary ops, unary negation, parens), input lengths 5 chars to 4.8MB; (2) 5,372 real Java 6 source files from the Spring framework (avg 3.8KiB, max 76KiB, comments stripped).
claimed_speedup: For the arithmetic-expression grammar, the paper states pika parsing was 'roughly the same speed' as ANTLR4/Parboiled2 for small inputs but became '10 times faster than ANTLR4' and '1000 times faster than Parboiled2' for large expressions (ANTLR4 scaled as ~n^1.21, Parboiled2 as ~n^1.9, pika as linear). For the Java grammar, the relationship reverses: the paper states pika parsing was 'up to 1000, 100 or 10 times slower' than ANTLR4 depending on input length, and about 100x slower than Parboiled2, because of a large per-character constant-factor overhead on complex grammars.
hardware: Ryzen 1800X CPU, single-threaded, JRE 13.0.2.
tradeoffs: Result is strongly grammar-dependent: faster than ANTLR4/Parboiled2 only for simple/shallow grammars (expression grammar) and markedly slower for large, deeply-nested grammars like Java's; pika parsing's benefit is mainly linear-time guarantee plus built-in left-recursion support and syntax-error recovery, not raw speed on complex languages; memoizes every rule at every position, which costs memory.
caveats: Not a universal speed win -- the same paper shows it is slower than both baselines on the Java grammar; the repository's public test suite (src/test/java/pikaparser/Benchmark.java) reproduces the Parboiled2 comparison, but no ANTLR4 comparison harness was found in the same repo, so the ANTLR4 numbers are not independently re-runnable from this exact codebase; published at SLE 2020 (peer-reviewed workshop), keeping it at tier B rather than A.

name: SafeRE
workload: JMH microbenchmarks: 150-row real-world matrix (25 patterns x match/no-match x 1K/10K/100K input sizes), plus 8 'Core' and 8 'Application' workloads, run against java.util.regex (JDK), RE2/J, RE2-FFM (Java FFM binding to native C++ RE2), native C++ RE2, PCRE2 JIT, Go regexp, Rust regex crate, and .NET's non-backtracking engine.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean 2.22x faster than JDK java.util.regex on the 150-row real-world matrix (1.88x after removing 2 pathological backtracking rows), but 22% slower than JDK on the smaller 'Core' set and 7% slower on 'Application'. Also 12.5x faster than RE2/J and 3.06x faster than RE2-FFM on the real-world matrix. However, against the three canonical native baselines it directly benchmarked: SafeRE is 13% slower than native C++ RE2, takes 2.47x as long as PCRE2 JIT, and takes 2.03x as long as Rust's regex crate on the same 150-row matrix (though 1.32x faster than native RE2 on the smaller 'Core' subset).
compiler_and_flags: Java: OpenJDK 26.0.2+10-55 targeting Java 21, JMH 1.37 (2 forks, 2 warmup iters x500ms, 5 measurement iters x500ms); C++: g++ 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG, RE2 snapshot 2025-11-05; PCRE2 10.47 with JIT enabled; Go 1.26.1 linux/amd64; Rust rustc 1.97.1 with regex 1.13.1; .NET SDK 10.0.110
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700K, 8 cores/16 threads, 3.6 GHz base, 16 GiB RAM under WSL2, Ubuntu 24.04 on Windows 11 host, Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2
tradeoffs: 71.2x slower to compile a pattern than the JDK (11.7x slower than RE2/J), and retains substantially more memory per compiled pattern, in exchange for guaranteed linear-time matching with no catastrophic-backtracking risk (e.g. 0.089us vs the JDK's 17,079us on an adversarial pattern). Cross-runtime ratios mix FFI/marshalling overhead with engine cost, so they are not pure same-runtime comparisons.
caveats: SafeRE is a from-scratch Java port of RE2's design (not a GitHub fork), so is_fork_of is null even though it is explicitly 'based on RE2'. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION because the LICENSE file is a compound notice, but the file text states both RE2 and RE2/J (and by extension this port) are BSD-3-Clause. Critically, on the primary 150-row real-world matrix, SafeRE is NOT faster than any of the three named baselines it tested that are on our incumbent list (RE2, PCRE2, Rust regex) -- it is slower than all three there; its clear win is only over java.util.regex, which is a widely used incumbent but not one of PCRE2/RE2/std::regex/Rust regex. This is an unusually rigorous, self-critical benchmark report (authors explicitly flag their own losses), which raises confidence in the numbers despite the mixed result.

name: re2jit
workload: Repo-bundled perf tests: a small Markdown-to-HTML converter using two regexes with capture groups (make test/32-markdownish), and a tokenizer for the 'dg' language whose pattern relies on a Unicode class equivalent to \w (make test/30-long), comparing re2jit's JIT-compiled Thompson-NFA-to-x86-64 approach against google/re2 directly.
claimed_speedup: Exactly as fast as RE2 for simple unanchored search with discarded groups (falls back to RE2's own DFA); 20-30% faster than RE2 when capture-group boundaries must be reported; up to 100x faster than RE2 on patterns using full Unicode character classes (e.g. \pL), because re2jit matches a whole code point via a 2-stage lookup table instead of RE2's enumerated-alternation expansion.
tradeoffs: x86-64 only (hand-written asm64 DSL that JIT-compiles into mmapped executable memory); does not implement \b/\B word boundaries at all; reserves Unicode plane-15 private-use code points internally. Backreferences are supported with a guaranteed-linear-time fast path when no backreferenced group is repeated, exponential otherwise (same as general backreference semantics).
caveats: First-party claim in the README with no CPU model, compiler, or exact timing numbers given (only percentage/multiplier ranges and 'run this make target yourself'), so capped at tier C. Project is abandoned since 2016 (>3 years, tagged per DO-NOT-EXCLUDE rules rather than skipped) and the author's own README notes that 'new versions of re2 have significantly improved Unicode charclass performance,' meaning the up-to-100x figure is very likely stale and would be much smaller against current RE2.

name: SeekStorm
workload: BM25 lexical search on English Wikipedia (5,032,105 docs, 8.28GB decompressed) using AOL-query-derived intersection/union/frequent-term/phrase queries, single-threaded, via the open-source 'search-benchmark-game' harness (forked from Tantivy/Jason Wolfe's benchmark)
claimed_speedup: vs Lucene: 4.6x-10.1x on typical single/multi-field 'all', 'union' and 'intersection' queries; up to 174.8x-734.1x on pathological single-very-frequent-term ('the') and two-phase-critic queries (vs Tantivy: 1x-6.1x typical, up to ~835x on the same frequent-term queries)
hardware: ThinkPad P1, 64.0 GB RAM, Intel Core i7-13700H 2.40GHz, 2TB Hynix NVMe SSD (per the Dec 2023 blog post). A later re-run of the same open-source search-benchmark-game harness, documented in github.com/SeekStorm/search-benchmark-game (README), used the same ThinkPad P1 Gen 6 / i7-13700H under Ubuntu 24.04 with Rust 1.90 and OpenJDK 21, but that run's raw results (results.json, versions tantivy-0.25/lucene-10.3.0-bp/seekstorm-1.0.0) were not re-aggregated into summary multipliers by us.
tradeoffs: Rust, single binary, no JVM/segment-merge GC pauses (claimed benefit for tail latency); newer project than Lucene/Tantivy with a smaller ecosystem and fewer production deployments; benchmark adapters are written by each engine's own authors ('for maximum authenticity') rather than a fully neutral third party.
caveats: Headline numbers are from a Dec 2023 first-party blog post using older engine versions, not the current results.json in the SeekStorm/search-benchmark-game repo. The extreme 100-800x multipliers occur only on a single very-frequent term ('the') and a two-term phrase+filter query, and plausibly reflect algorithmic handling of very common terms (block-max pruning) rather than a general throughput advantage; typical multi-term intersection/union queries show a much more modest 1.6x-10.1x edge over Lucene. Exact compiler flags for the JVM (Lucene) and rustc (SeekStorm) build are not stated on the cited page, so tier is capped at B rather than A.

name: frg (fastripgrep)
workload: 8 regex/literal/alternation/wildcard patterns searched over the openclaw codebase (9,000 files), case-sensitive, warm cache, output to /dev/null, comparing frg's sparse n-gram index against ripgrep and grep.
claimed_speedup: 5.3x faster than ripgrep on a selective literal search (10ms vs 53ms); wins on all 8 tested pattern types vs ripgrep (1.06x-5.3x); up to ~150x faster than grep on the same literal pattern (1553ms vs 10ms); 100% match-count parity with ripgrep
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release; no rustc version or CPU-specific flags stated
tradeoffs: Requires an upfront index build (~20-23s for 9K files; incremental updates ~70ms via overlay/tombstone); index must be kept in sync (frg update/watch); adds a .frg/ directory to the repo tree; falls back to brute-force scan for patterns with no extractable literals.
caveats: First-party README benchmark only. CPU model and Rust toolchain version are not stated, so despite public bench code (benches/bench.rs) this falls short of tier A. Not stated how many repeats each row reflects.

name: ngi (N-gram Indexed Regex Search)
workload: 5 regex patterns (attribute macros, function calls, struct names, exported symbols, mutex usage) searched across the Linux kernel source tree (92,916 files) using ngi's trigram index + ripgrep verification, compared against plain ripgrep and grep -r.
claimed_speedup: 1.7x-5.9x faster than ripgrep and 13x-69x faster than grep across the 5 tested patterns on the Linux kernel (e.g. 27ms vs rg's 161ms vs grep's 1866ms for `__attribute__.*section`); 100% match parity with ripgrep (13/13 test queries)
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release; no CPU model or rustc version stated
tradeoffs: Falls back to a full ripgrep scan when more than ~10% of files match a query (index only helps selective queries); index build takes ~16s for the Linux kernel and produces a 146MB index that must be kept current; depends on ripgrep being on PATH for best performance (falls back to a built-in Rust regex engine otherwise).
caveats: First-party README benchmark on a fixed, named corpus (Linux kernel) with a reproducible pattern list, but hardware/CPU model and exact toolchain version are not stated, so it falls short of tier A.

name: ugrep (with ugrep-indexer)
workload: Cold-filesystem recursive search for the pattern 'std::chrono' across the ugrep v3.12.6 source tree (1,317 files, 28 directories, 12.2MB), with OS file-system cache cleared by unmounting/remounting the drive; 8 threads
claimed_speedup: README states ugrep's own indexed cold search (0.0487s best-of-4, range 0.0487-0.0983s) is '21 times faster' (10x-21x across runs) than ugrep's own unindexed cold search (1.02s); ripgrep 13.0.0 took 1.18s on the same cold search, i.e. roughly 12x-24x faster than ripgrep for the indexed run (derived from page data). Without indexing, plain ugrep (1.02s) was already marginally faster than ripgrep (1.18s) on this query.
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (ugrep); ugrep-indexer companion tool is a separate, smaller repo (84 stars)
tradeoffs: Speed advantage requires running the separate ugrep-indexer tool ahead of time to build per-directory N-gram Bloom-filter index files (~4KB/file storage overhead at default accuracy, tunable 0-9); index has a false-positive rate so some non-matching files are still opened; benefit is specific to cold/uncached file systems -- on a warm page cache, indexed search adds overhead and may not be faster; index must be kept up to date (incremental re-indexing) as files change.
caveats: Numbers come from the project's own README with exact commands shown, but no CPU model, OS, or compiler flags are stated, and the dataset is small (1,317 files); this caps the tier at C rather than A/B. The '21x' figure as stated compares indexed vs. ugrep's own unindexed run, not directly vs. ripgrep -- the ~12x-24x vs-ripgrep figure is derived by us from the same page's numbers.

name: libucl
workload: Parse and emit a 19 MB JSON file of about 700 thousand lines generated with json-generator.com, timing the whole-file parse and each emit format.
claimed_speedup: Parse: jansson 1.3899 s vs UCL 0.6649 s (about 2.1x, derived from page data); UCL built with -O3 parses in 0.3002 s (about 4.6x vs the jansson figure, derived from page data, but the jansson figure is not stated to be -O3). Emit: jansson 0.2609 s vs UCL config 0.2423 s, JSON 0.2329 s, compact JSON 0.1811 s, YAML 0.2489 s (about 1.1x for JSON, derived from page data); UCL -O3 emit 0.1174 s config and JSON, 0.0991 s compact JSON, 0.1354 s YAML.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the jansson run. The first UCL set is described only as unoptimized, the second as 'compiled with optimizations (-O3)'.
tradeoffs: UCL is a configuration language that is a superset of JSON (macros, includes, variables, comments, implicit arrays, multiple values per key, JSON Schema v4 validation) with CBOR and MessagePack input and output, so the parse does more than plain JSON. The README warns that with all features enabled it is meant for trusted configuration input only and must not take adversarial input. C API with an object tree; zero-copy parsing is an opt-in flag (UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY). Bindings for Lua, Python and Haskell live in the repo.
caveats: First-party README numbers from one run on one generated file: no CPU, OS, compiler version, jansson version or jansson build flags are given, and the two UCL sets differ in optimization level, so the unoptimized and -O3 ratios mix builds. tests/test_speed.c in the repo times only UCL (it mmaps the file and uses UCL_PARSER_ZEROCOPY); the jansson harness is not in the repo, so the comparison is not reproducible from public code. The README does not say whether the quoted run used the zero-copy flag, which would favour UCL over jansson (which allocates its own strings). The emit gap against jansson is small. The benchmark harness source carries a 2013 copyright header, so the numbers are probably old. No independent benchmark including libucl was found.
